claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles depends systematically on particle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower thermal stability than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower effective thermal conductivity than larger particles.
The as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are disordered random solid solutions.
MD can calculate thermal conductivity and track atomic displacements or structural evolution in a high-entropy alloy.
Heating the simulated nanoparticles above transformation temperatures will induce significant atomic mobility or melting.
Smaller nanoparticles have a greater surface-to-volume ratio.
A greater surface-to-volume ratio produces a higher proportion of under-coordinated atoms.
Under-coordinated surface atoms mediate atomic displacements and defect formation.
Enhanced surface effects in smaller nanoparticles reduce cohesive energy.
Enhanced surface effects promote atomic diffusion in smaller nanoparticles.
Reduced cohesive energy and enhanced diffusion cause structural changes to begin at lower temperatures in smaller nanoparticles.
Surface-mediated structural changes lower the effective thermal conductivity of smaller nanoparticles.
Larger nanoparticles retain more bulk-like intrinsic lattice properties because they have a greater bulk fraction.
Changes in atomic ordering and displacement can be associated with changes in lattice thermal conductivity in an HEA.
Particles below 5 nm or above 50 nm may deviate from the predicted size trend because different phenomena could dominate.
The quantitative size dependence is sensitive to the selected interatomic potential and nanoscale surface effects.
